summary: A revision of the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, the way one computer asks another to send or receive files. It came out of months of discussion in RFCs and a committee meeting at BBN, and changes the previous official version while keeping its overall structure. It was replaced by RFC 765.

plainLanguage.summary: This version of FTP lets a program request file operations on another ARPANET host. Commands travel on a control connection, while file contents travel over a separate data connection.

subtitle: The 1973 ARPANET FTP revision separates command control from file data transfer.

tldr.problem: ARPANET hosts had different file systems, and the previous official FTP version needed changes after working-group discussions.
tldr.mechanism: A user protocol interpreter sends commands over a TELNET connection; separate data connections transfer files using selected representation, structure, and transmission modes.
tldr.outcome: The preface planned a move from temporary Socket 21 to Socket 3 on 1 February 1974. The RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 765 and updated by RFCs 614 and 640.

today: RFC 542 is a historical FTP specification, obsoleted by RFC 765. The metadata also lists updates by RFC 614 and RFC 640.

sections.title: FTP's Purpose and Model
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) moves files between Hosts on the ARPA Computer Network. Its goals include file sharing, remote use of storage, and hiding differences among hosts' file systems.

A user-side protocol interpreter sends commands over a TELNET connection to the server. The server replies and directs a data transfer process; file contents travel over a separate data connection. FTP can also arrange a transfer between two servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A client sends file commands to a server over one connection. The file itself moves over a separate data connection, which may be opened only when needed.

sections.title: Representation and Data Connections
sections.content:
FTP lets a user select a representation type such as ASCII, EBCDIC, Image, or Local byte, and a file structure such as file or record structure. The chosen representation can transform data between a host's storage form and its transfer form.

The user can set a transfer byte size, which defaults to 8 bits, and select the data socket. The server normally initiates the data connection. A transfer may use one of three modes: Stream sends bytes, Block sends headed data blocks, and Compressed encodes runs of data or filler.
sections.plainLanguage: The two hosts agree how bytes represent the file, whether it contains records, and how to send it. They can send a stream, labelled blocks, or compressed data.

sections.title: Restarting Interrupted Transfers
sections.content:
FTP does not detect bits lost or scrambled during transfer; the RFC says that issue may be handled at the NCP level. It does define restart procedures for Block and Compressed modes.

The sender inserts a marker into the data stream, and the receiver records its corresponding position. After a system failure, the user sends a restart command with the server's marker, followed immediately by the interrupted service command.
sections.plainLanguage: Block and Compressed transfers can include markers that identify a checkpoint. After a system failure, the user can request a restart from a recorded marker.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
FTP commands are TELNET strings that end with the TELNET end-of-line code. Commands cover access identifiers, transfer parameters, and file services such as retrieve, store, append, rename, delete, and list. The user initiates the control connection to the server's standard socket 3.

The server replies with a three-digit code and explanatory text. The first digit groups replies: 2xx indicates a positive acknowledgment, 3xx requires more information, 4xx means the server could not fulfil a correctly specified request, and 5xx means the command is incorrect or illegal.

The preface says the new version would temporarily use socket 21 and move to socket 3 on 1 February 1974.
sections.plainLanguage: The user sends short commands, and the server replies with a code and text. The first digit indicates success, a need for more information, an unsuccessful request, or an invalid command.
